title: Distributions an analyst meets
reading_md:
**What it is.** Data come in a few shapes, and the shape decides which summary and which test fit.

- Roughly normal: averages of many observations, thanks to the central limit theorem. The theorem is about the average, not the data themselves.
- Skewed with a long right tail: order values, revenue, time on site.
- Zero-inflated: revenue per visitor, where most visitors buy nothing.
- Discrete and bounded: counts such as orders per hour (whole numbers, 0 or more) and rates such as conversion (between 0% and 100%).

**How to work it out.**

Revenue per visitor = conversion rate × average order value

Worked example. 1,000 visitors, 30 buyers, an average order of €80.

- Revenue = 30 × 80 = €2,400.
- Revenue per visitor = 2,400 / 1,000 = €2.40 (2 decimals). The same as 3% × €80.
- Share of visitors with zero revenue = 970 / 1,000 = 97%.

Averaging only over the 30 buyers gives €80, the average order value, not revenue per visitor.

**In the interview.** "Why is revenue per visitor harder to test than conversion rate?" A model answer: "It is skewed and mostly zeros, so its variance is high and a test needs more data to detect the same change. I would split it into conversion rate and average order value, and test each."

**Common mistakes.**

- Assuming revenue is normally distributed.
- Believing the central limit theorem makes the data normal. On large samples it makes the mean roughly normal; the order values stay skewed.
- Ignoring the zeros when averaging.
